metaDescription: Saw an edit credited to ghaus editz? Grab the right AI prompt above, paste it into Gemini or ChatGPT with your photo, and remake that viral look yourself.
bodyHtml:
If you typed ai prompt ghaus editz into a search bar, you almost certainly saw a reel or short with that handle stamped in the corner, liked the edit, and went looking for the recipe. That is how a lot of people shop for prompts now. A look goes around, someone gets the credit tag, and the rest of us try to reverse engineer it. I will be straight with you upfront: I do not know who is behind that handle, and I am not going to make up a backstory. What I can do is help you get the same kind of viral AI edits using the prompts sitting in the grid above this article.

A handle is shorthand for a look, not a secret AI prompt

When a name like this trends, people start treating it like a password. They think if they just find the exact account or the exact caption, the edit will fall into their lap. It almost never works that way. The handle is a label your memory attached to a style. The actual edit is a short instruction plus a source photo plus two or three retries. Once you accept that, you stop chasing one account and start describing the result you want.

So before you copy anything, look hard at the edit that pulled you in. Most viral AI edits are doing one or two obvious things, and the rest is polish.

  • A new background: a temple, a rainy street, a studio backdrop, a field at golden hour.
  • A style swap: 3D figurine, oil painting, polaroid, retro film, comic ink.
  • A light change: hard side light, soft glow, neon rim light, moody low key.
  • An outfit or era change: traditional wear, 90s Bollywood, vintage suit.

What is trending in AI prompt edits right now

The looks that travel fastest on reels and shorts tend to cluster. I keep seeing the same handful, and they are easy to reproduce once you name them plainly. The tiny 3D figurine of yourself on a desk is still everywhere. So is the retro saree or sherwani portrait with grainy film color. Polaroid-style couple shots, the cinematic HDR headshot with sharp eyes, and the toy-box or action-figure packaging gag all keep coming back around.

Most of these are made with Google's Gemini image model, the one people nicknamed nano banana. It handles photo edits, portraits, couple shots, and figurine looks well, it is free to try in the Gemini app, and it costs only a few cents an image through the API. ChatGPT with its image tool, Midjourney, and DALL-E can hit similar territory, but for the face-keeping edits that go viral, Gemini is usually the one people reach for first.

Match the style to an AI prompt, not one account

Here is the part that saves you time. Two creators can land the identical edit with completely different wording, and any one creator changes their phrasing constantly. Hunting for one person's exact sentence is the slow road. Describe the look, grab the closest prompt above, and tune it to your own photo. You will usually beat the original anyway because you are fitting it to your face, not theirs.

Edit you sawDescribe it asThen add
Tiny 3D figurine of youCollectible figure on a desk, plastic finish, soft studio lightKeep the face, add a base or box
Retro Bollywood portraitFaded film color, grain, warm tungsten light, vintage wardrobeName a decade like the 90s
Cinematic HDR headshotSharp eyes, crisp detail, dramatic side light, plain backgroundAsk for natural skin, not plastic
Polaroid couple shotInstant film border, slight blur, flash look, cozy moodSet the pose and the setting

How to write an AI prompt that actually works

The mistake most people make is dumping ten adjectives and hoping. Be specific about the few things that carry the look, then let the model fill the gaps. A prompt that works reads like a clear instruction you could say to a friend who edits photos.

  1. Open the edit you liked and pick the two or three things that make it work.
  2. Copy the nearest prompt from the grid above this article.
  3. Paste it into Gemini or ChatGPT and upload your own photo.
  4. Tell it plainly what to keep: the face, the pose, the hair.
  5. Change one detail at a time and regenerate until it matches.

That last step matters more than people think. If you rewrite the whole prompt every try, you never learn which word moved the result. Change the light, run it. Change the background, run it. You build a feel for the model fast that way.

Tip: keep a notes file of the exact lines that gave you a clean result. After a week you will have your own small prompt kit, which beats any single screenshot you saved from someone else.

Common AI prompt mistakes and quick fixes

Most edits that come out wrong fail for boring, fixable reasons. None of this is about a missing magic word.

  • Face changes too much: add a line telling it to preserve the original face and identity, and use a clear, well lit source photo.
  • Skin looks like plastic: ask for natural skin texture and remove words like flawless or perfect.
  • Hands or text come out mangled: keep them out of frame when you can, or crop tighter on the face.
  • The vibe is close but flat: name the light source and time of day, which does more than any color word.
  • It ignores your edit: shorten the prompt. Long, contradictory prompts confuse the model more than they help.

The source photo does half the AI prompt work

People obsess over wording and ignore the photo they feed in, which is backwards. A clean input gets you most of the way before the prompt does anything. If the model has a sharp, evenly lit face to work from, it keeps your features and the edit lands. If you hand it a dark, blurry crop, no prompt rescues it.

  • Use a front-facing or slight-angle shot where both eyes are visible.
  • Shoot in soft, even light. Window light beats a phone flash.
  • Fill the frame with the face and shoulders, not a tiny figure in the distance.
  • Skip heavy beauty filters on the input. The model edits cleaner skin worse, and you lose your real texture.
  • For couple or group edits, give it a photo where everyone is already in frame rather than asking it to add a person.

One more thing on this. These edits put your face into new scenes, so use your own photos and think before posting an edit of someone who did not agree to it. The tools make it easy to forget that a real person is in the picture.

A realistic AI prompt example walkthrough

Say the edit you saw was a moody temple-step portrait in warm evening light. You would start from a portrait prompt in the grid, upload a clear photo of yourself, and write something like: keep my face and pose, place me sitting on old stone temple steps at sunset, warm side light, soft shadows, natural skin, slight film grain. Run it. If the face drifts, add a stronger keep-the-face line. If it looks too clean, push the grain and warmth. Four or five passes and you have something you can post, with your own face, not a name with no prompt behind it.

That is the whole game. The handle got you curious, but the prompt above plus your photo plus a few honest retries is what actually puts the edit on your feed. Start with the closest match in the grid and shape it from there.

faqs.a: I do not have verified information about who runs that handle, and I am not going to invent any. People mostly search it after seeing an AI edit credited to that name and wanting the same look. The practical move is to describe the edit you liked and match it to one of the prompts in the grid above.

faqs.q: How do I get the exact prompt ghaus editz used?
faqs.a: Usually you cannot. Creators rarely publish their real wording and change it constantly. You also do not need it. Name the background, light, and style of the edit in plain words, copy the closest prompt here, paste it with your own photo, and tweak one detail at a time until it matches.

faqs.q: What AI tool makes these viral edits?
faqs.a: Most of them come from Google's Gemini image model, nicknamed nano banana, which is free to try in the Gemini app and a few cents per image through the API. ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL-E can do similar work, but for edits that keep your real face, Gemini is the usual first pick.

faqs.q: Why do I get prompts when I search a creator name?
faqs.a: Because freepromptbase is a prompt library, not a profile directory. When a search is really a creator handle, we point you to prompts that produce that style. You came for a look, and the prompts above are the fastest way to make it yourself with your own photo.

faqs.q: Why does the edit change my face so much?
faqs.a: Almost always the source photo or the prompt. Use a clear, well lit photo and add an explicit line telling the model to keep your original face and identity. Drop words like flawless and perfect, ask for natural skin texture, and keep the prompt short so it does not fight itself.
